item_name: Tschopp Reiser Turaga 2018 connectome-constrained object tracking (arXiv 1806.04793)
bibliography: Primary: Fabian David Tschopp (Institute of Neuroinformatics, UZH/ETH Zurich), Michael B. Reiser, Srinivas C. Turaga (Janelia Research Campus, HHMI). 'A Connectome Based Hexagonal Lattice Convolutional Network Model of the Drosophila Visual System'. arXiv:1806.04793 [q-bio.NC]. v1 submitted 12 Jun 2018 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04793v1, PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04793v1); v2 submitted 24 Jun 2018, the current version (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04793v2). arXiv comment: 'Work in progress. Final paper with results from an updated model with new connectome data will be coming soon'. No journal reference and no DOI; the Janelia publication page lists it only as arXiv, 12 Jun 2018. The v1 PDF carries a NIPS 2017 (Long Beach) style-file footer. The NIPS 2017 proceedings do not contain this paper, so the footer most likely comes from the template or an unaccepted submission [uncertain]. Version differences, from a line diff of the two PDFs' text: v2 adds Figures 3-5 (synapse counts per neuron and edge; correlation of trained vs initial weights; DSI on the network graph), renumbers the later figures (v1 Fig 3-6 = v2 Fig 6-9) and replaces the NIPS footer with a link to the supplement. Methods text and all numbers are identical in v1 and v2. Supplementary repository: https://github.com/naibaf7/dvsc_2017_supplemental. It holds 4 files (nips_2017.pdf, which is the same paper text; supplemental.pdf, 34 pages; supp_clip_bar.mp4; supp_clip_davis.mp4) in 2 commits, with no source code, README or license. The paper describes the implementation as a custom Caffe layer, the 'sparse repeated pattern recurrent neural network' (SRPRNN Caffe, LibDNN), but no public code link is given. Successor from the same group: Lappalainen J.K., Tschopp F.D., Prakhya S., McGill M., Nern A., Shinomiya K., Takemura S., Gruntman E., Macke J.H., Turaga S.C. bioRxiv 2023, then Nature 2024, 'Connectome-constrained networks predict neural activity across the fly visual system' (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07939-3; code TuragaLab/flyvis). This is effectively the promised 'final paper', but it switched the task to optic flow on Sintel. It is a different study, not a duplicate record. Forward citations: Semantic Scholar lists 34 citing records and OpenAlex counts 23 (queried 2026-10-16). Notable ones: Lappalainen et al. 2023 bioRxiv / 2024 Nature (FlyVis); Linsley et al. 2021 NeurIPS 'Tracking Without Re-recognition in Humans and Machines' (cites it, but builds a separate cortical-style tracker); Litwin-Kumar & Turaga 2019 Curr Opin Neurobiol 'Constraining computational models using electron microscopy wiring diagrams'; Morra & Daley 2022/2023 IJCNN 'Using Connectome Features to Constrain Echo State Networks'; Hexagonal CNNs for Hexagonal Grids (IEEE Access 2019); 'The Understanding of ON-Edge Motion Detection Through the Simulation Based on the Connectome of Drosophila's Optic Lobe' (J Robotics Mechatronics 2022); 'Connecting Connectomes to Physiology' (J Neurosci 2023); 'Connectomics: relating synaptic connectivity to physiology' (Curr Biol 2022); 'Predicting Neural Activity from Connectome Embedding Spaces' (bioRxiv 2025); 'Connectomes inform function' (Natural Computing 2025); 'Connectome-based biophysical modeling of a figure-ground discrimination circuit' (bioRxiv 2026). Judging from titles only, no citing work reuses the connectome network for object tracking on natural video [uncertain]. A 2026 stress test of flyvis, Dhawan 'FlyHack: Stress-Testing Mechanistic Claims in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model' (arXiv 2610.13018), is relevant as a caution, but it is not confirmed to cite Tschopp 2018 [uncertain].
full_text_checked: Read in full: v2 PDF (14 pages: all sections, Figures 1-9 and their captions, references) and v1 PDF (compared with v2 by text diff). Figure 7 (left) was rendered and read visually to get per-configuration values, because the text gives only the best and worst numbers. Supplemental.pdf: read the implementation section (GTX 1080 throughput, 1183 synaptic weights, BPTT history) and skimmed the per-neuron filter and equation pages and the reference list. Not watched: the two supplement videos. Not available: training code, data split lists, per-run logs and seed information, because none are published.
task_and_output: Proxy task: single-object tracking framed as per-frame regression. A 3-layer fully connected decoder (128 -> 32 -> 4 units; 164 decoder neurons, Xavier init, unconstrained) reads the transmedullary output cells of the simulated lamina and medulla. It regresses 4 scalars: object centroid (x, y) and centroid velocity between consecutive frames (dx, dy), in ommatidia units (Section 3, Figure 2). Ground truth comes from DAVIS 2016 dense single-object segmentation masks. There is no heat map, no box or size, no presence score and no exemplar. The main scientific output is not tracking accuracy but the emergent tuning of model neurons (DSI and orientation selectivity of T4a-d and other types, Figures 8-9).
data_and_independent_videos: DAVIS 2016 at 480p (50 sequences, 40-100 frames, 24 FPS). Only 8 sequences were used: bmx-bumps, drift-chicane, motorbike, paragliding, rollerblade, soccerball, surf, kite-walk. They were chosen because they 'contain primarily object motion and maintain a static camera position' (Section 3.1). Each sequence was cut into blocks of 10 consecutive frames. Per sequence, 2 blocks (20 frames) went to test and the remaining 2-8 blocks to training, so train and test come from the SAME 8 videos. There is no unseen-video test. The training data were augmented by vertical and horizontal mirroring. Total test material is 8 x 20 = 160 frames. The block selection rule (random or fixed position) is not reported [uncertain].
target_size_and_input_resolution: Input lattice: 20 x 35 hexagonal columns, about 700 ommatidia, each spanning 5 degrees (Section 2). RGB frames are resampled to the hexagonal lattice (nearest-neighbour or bilinear 'ommatidia mode'): R1-R6 get grayscale, R7 red (as a UV proxy), and R8 30% blue / 70% green. Images are normalized and no spherical projection is simulated (Section 2.3). The model has 43 neuron types. Target size in ommatidia is NOT reported. Because the 480p frames are squeezed to 35 x 20 columns (about 24 px per column horizontally), the DAVIS foreground objects (bikers, cars, paragliders, a ball) would span roughly 1 to over 10 columns [uncertain: estimate, not from the paper].
frame_rate_and_camera_motion: Source video is 24 FPS. Simulation steps use arbitrary units, and velocity error is reported in 'ommatidia/step', which implies one frame per step [uncertain]. The camera is static by selection: sequences where the camera follows the object were excluded because relative object motion was near zero. There is therefore no ego-motion and the background is mostly static, apart from natural scene motion such as water, dust and spectators.
detector_and_exemplar: No detector and no exemplar or template. The single annotated object is implicitly 'the' target, and the network must regress its centroid and velocity from the whole field of view. There is no mechanism to specify which object to follow.
trainable_nodes_and_loss: Trained parts: all connectome edge weights (1183 synaptic weights according to the supplement; spatially shared like convolution filters), per-type biases (initialized to 3.5/75) and the decoder. Weights were initialized from synapse counts divided by 75. Signs were fixed from connectome and RNA-seq transmitter data and enforced by a projected update theta' = sign(theta0) * |theta|, which mirrors weights across 0 instead of zeroing them (Section 3.2). Neurons are leaky-ReLU point neurons with instantaneous synapses, plus 1-step delays on recurrent, feedback and autapse edges and selected physiological delays (e.g., T4 inputs). Training used BPTT with a history of 10 steps and a batch size of 5, Adam with weight decay, 30,000 iterations per configuration. Loss: squared error on object location and velocity (Section 3.2). In the 'untrained' control only the biases and the decoder are trained.
controls_seeds_splits: Six configurations (Section 3.2, Figure 7): (1) Takemura 2017 connectome init, trained; (2) Takemura 2017 + 40% uniform multiplicative noise, trained; (3) Takemura 2017 with weights fixed, only biases and decoder trained; (4) Random MSRA init with connectome signs, trained; (5) Random + 40% multiplicative noise, trained; (6) Takemura 2013 (older T4 input model), trained. Missing controls: no shuffled or rewired connectome at the same sparsity, no unconstrained CNN or RNN baseline of equal size, no trivial baselines (frame centre, previous position, constant velocity) and no decoder-only-on-pixels baseline. Seeds: one run per configuration as far as reported; no seed count, no repeated runs. Error bars in Figure 7 are unexplained (probably variation over test samples) [uncertain]. Split: within-video temporal blocks (see data field).
metrics_and_numbers: Metric: mean L2 error in ommatidia on the test blocks (20 frames from each of the 8 sequences), for position and for velocity (Figure 7 left; Section 4.1). Text, Section 4.1: best position error 'as low as 2.0 ommatidia'; the fixed-connectome (untrained-weights) network was worst at 2.6 ommatidia; velocity errors 0.28-0.33 ommatidia/step across configurations. Per configuration, read visually from the Figure 7 bars (approximate, +/-0.05) [uncertain]: Takemura 2017 untrained about 2.65; Takemura 2017 trained about 2.02; Takemura 2017 + 40% noise about 2.43; Takemura 2013 trained about 2.01; Random trained about 2.37; Random + 40% noise about 2.13. Error bars are roughly +/-0.2-0.25 and overlap between all trained configurations. In Figure 7, Random + 40% noise (about 2.13) beats Takemura 2017 + 40% noise (about 2.43) and is within the error bars of the best connectome model. So the paper does NOT show a tracking-accuracy advantage from connectome initialization. The authors say so themselves: 'networks initialized with random weights were also able to track objects' (Section 4.3). The only accuracy contrast shown is that training the core weights (about 2.0) beat fixing them (2.6), about a 24% lower error, with one run each. Tuning results: Figures 8e-f and 9 show T4a-d become direction selective at 192, 359, 51 and 275 degrees with two-lobed orientation selectivity only in connectome-initialized trained networks. Random-init networks did not recover T4 tuning (Figures 8g-h); instead other neurons, such as T3 at 10 degrees and L4 at 238 degrees, became selective, and with 40% noise L2 and Tm6 did (Section 4.3). The connectome solution was robust to 40% initialization noise. T5 tuning was not recovered (T5a selective at 335 degrees instead of about 180). Figure 4 shows ON-pathway weights largely unchanged by training and OFF-pathway weights changed. Figure 7 (right) shows that trained connectome and random solutions differ in their weights. Implementation (supplement Figure 1): up to about 15e10 synapse updates/s on a GTX 1080.
tested_conditions: Unseen videos: NO (test blocks come from the same 8 training sequences). Target absence: NO (the object is always present, and there is no presence output). Similar distractors: NO (single-object DAVIS 2016; distractors are not discussed). Occlusion: NOT REPORTED (DAVIS 2016 contains some partial occlusions, but they are not analysed). Night or low light: NO. Sequential operation on own predictions: NO (open-loop regression from ground-truth frames in 10-frame blocks; no crop that follows the prediction and no track state). Camera motion: NO (static-camera sequences selected on purpose). Multiple objects: NO.
mechanism_summary: Published mechanism: a hexagonal-lattice recurrent convolutional network whose cell types, connectivity pattern, signs and initial weights come from lamina and medulla EM connectomes (43 types, about 700 columns). It is trained end to end with BPTT, through a small MLP decoder, to regress one object's centroid and velocity on static-camera natural video. The paper's claim concerns neuroscience, not tracking: connectome initialization plus task training makes T4 cells acquire their known direction and orientation tuning, which random initialization with the same signs does not do. The tracking accuracy is essentially the same for connectome and random initialization, and training the core weights beats freezing them. No claim is made about identity, distractor rejection or refusal. Any use for target re-identification would be our proposed modification, not a published mechanism.
transfer_limits: (1) Frame rate and motion: 24 FPS, static camera, no ego-motion. Our setting is 30 Hz with a moving and rescaling crop centred on the track prediction, so the core sees mostly self-induced background motion that their data excluded on purpose. (2) Input: about 700 colour-split ommatidia over the full frame, versus our 721 grey hexals over a crop. Their colour channels (R7/R8) carried information that our gray input lacks. The scale is similar, but our target fills a known large part of the crop (about 9.4 x 12.1 lattice steps), while their target size is unreported. Their 2.0-ommatidia error relative to a target of unknown size cannot be compared with our useful-correction criterion. (3) Task: single object, always present, no exemplar, no refusal. This is the opposite of Z13 (find the previous target among similar neighbours, using an exemplar of 4 observations, or refuse). Nothing in the paper informs discrimination between similar objects or abstention. (4) Evaluation: 160 test frames from the 8 videos seen in training, a single run per configuration, unexplained error bars, and no trivial baselines. The 2.0 vs 2.6 'train the core' gain is not statistically established and was not tested on unseen videos, unlike our paired bootstrap over val videos. (5) Open loop: there is no closed-loop operation in which the network's output moves its own input window, which is exactly where our errors compound. (6) Environment: no detector or association stage. Its relevance to YOLO/ByteTrack/MASA is only the choice of a readout node, with no evidence about the tracker. (7) Architecture: the model is a ReLU point-neuron network, not FlyVis's continuous-time dynamics with time constants. The weight and parameter counts differ (1183 edge weights here vs 734 type-level parameters in FlyVis).
research_questions_addressed: Q1 (exemplar-based recognition among similar objects and refusal): no direct evidence. The source has no exemplar, distractors or absence. It is a caution against citing it as connectome-based object tracking with re-identification ability. Q2 (representation vs readout vs training): weak direct evidence of design relevance. The paper has exactly the control family we need: a fixed connectome core with trained biases and decoder (2.6) vs a trained core (about 2.0) vs a random-init core with matching signs, trained (about 2.1-2.4). It shows that core training mattered more than anatomy for task accuracy, from single runs on in-video test blocks. This supports adding a sign-matched random or shuffled FlyVis core control to our B/C/D comparison. Q3 (target size, resolution, frame rate, camera motion): caution. 24 FPS and a static camera, chosen deliberately, so it gives no support for moving crops at 30 Hz. Q4 (joint position and refusal): not addressed. Q5 (separating FlyVis contribution from readout and training): design analogy. It provides a ready-made template of controls (frozen core, random-init core, noise-perturbed init) and a warning that equal task scores across initializations are expected ('many local minima'). A FlyVis contribution should therefore be claimed only if the connectome-initialized core beats a matched random or shuffled core under equal training.
candidate_node_change: The source suggests no new node change beyond what the project already did: training core weights through an object loss with sign constraints corresponds to our variant D, and FlyVis already fixes signs from the connectome. Its useful contribution is the missing control. Proposed check (core node, no new mechanism): add variant D-rand, a FlyVis-architecture core with connectome signs and connectivity kept, but magnitudes re-initialized at random (MSRA-like) or shuffled across edges of the same sign and type pair. Train it with the identical Z13 readout, loss, budget and steps as D. Comparisons on the same observations: B (no FlyVis, about 9602 params), C (frozen stock FlyVis), D (FlyVis-init core trained), D-rand (random-init core of the same architecture, trained), all with the same about 11,746-param readout. Minimal check: about 500 steps x 3 seeds per variant on the existing Z13 train cache; evaluate the useful-centre rate and refusal AUROC/AURC on held-out val videos with paired bootstrap over videos. Only after this, and only for the winner, run one HOTA run. Stop condition, written before the run: if D minus D-rand on the useful-centre rate has a 95% CI that includes 0 (or D-rand is better), drop any claim that the FlyVis connectome itself helps Z13. If D also does not beat B, stop core training for Z13 and treat the gain as a readout or architecture effect (rule 6.16: result (3) must beat (2)). Cost: hours of GPU, within budget [uncertain: estimate].
strongest_objection: This is a 2018 'work in progress' preprint that was never peer-reviewed. Its tracking result rests on 8 static-camera videos, tested on blocks of the same videos, with one run per configuration, no trivial baselines and only bar-chart numbers. By its own account, random initialization tracked about as well as the connectome, so it gives no evidence that fly anatomy helps object localization, let alone re-identification among similar distractors or refusal. The authors' own follow-up (Lappalainen et al. 2024) dropped the tracking task in favour of optic flow. Citing it as support for a FlyVis object readout in a multi-object tracker would overstate it. At most it supports the methodological point that core training and matched random-core controls must be reported.
evidence_strength: Weak. arXiv preprint (v1/v2, June 2018), labelled 'work in progress'; not peer-reviewed. No independent replication of the tracking result. The successor FlyVis paper is peer-reviewed (Nature 2024) but uses a different task. No code is released: the supplement repository contains only PDFs and videos (verified 2026-10-16). Single run per configuration, test data from the training videos, and per-configuration numbers available only as figure bars. The neuroscience claim (T4 tuning emerges only from connectome init) is better supported than any tracking claim, but it also rests on single runs.
